clean-desk.summary: Your desk is a data source. Documents left out, credentials written on sticky notes, or a screen left unlocked when you step away can expose sensitive information just as effectively as a cyberattack — sometimes more so. A clean desk policy isn't about tidiness. It's about ensuring the information you're responsible for doesn't become accessible to the wrong person.

story.title: The sticky note that cost a company millions
story.meta: Physical security · Clean desk · Credential exposure
story.text:
In 2019, a financial services firm experienced a significant data breach — not through hacking, but through a single Post-it note. An employee had written their system login credentials on a note stuck to their monitor. A contractor working in the building after hours photographed it with their phone. Within 48 hours, the contractor had accessed client financial records affecting thousands of accounts.

The employee hadn't done anything malicious. They were just trying to remember a complex password. But one small habit — one piece of paper — opened a door that cost the company $4.2 million in breach notifications, legal fees, and remediation.

The irony? The company had sophisticated cybersecurity controls in place. Their firewall, their MFA, their email filtering — all working perfectly. None of it mattered because someone wrote a password on a sticky note.

redFlags: Passwords, PINs, or access codes written anywhere on or near your desk — sticky notes, notebooks, whiteboards
Sensitive documents left face-up on your desk when you step away, even briefly
Your computer screen unlocked and visible when you're not at it
Confidential printouts left sitting in the printer or on a shared workspace
Visitor or contractor access to areas where sensitive materials are visible
Personal devices (phones, USB drives) left plugged into work computers unattended
responseSteps: Lock your screen every single time you leave your desk — no exceptions (Windows: Win+L, Mac: Cmd+Ctrl+Q). Make it muscle memory.
Never write passwords down anywhere. Use an approved password manager instead — see the Password Hygiene module.
File, shred, or lock away sensitive documents before leaving for the day. Nothing confidential stays on your desk overnight.
Collect printouts immediately after printing. Never leave confidential documents sitting in a shared printer.
When working in open spaces or coffee shops, position your monitor so it cannot be seen by people passing by — or use a privacy screen.
If you spot sensitive information left unattended by a colleague, let them know privately — it helps everyone.
endOfDayChecklist: Sensitive documents filed, shredded, or locked away
Printed materials collected — nothing left in the printer
Notebook or paper with any notes containing sensitive information stored securely
USB drives, access cards, and physical tokens put away
Desk clear of anything you wouldn't want a stranger to read

publicSpaces.title: Working in public spaces
points: In cafes, airports, or shared offices — position your screen so it faces a wall or away from foot traffic.
A privacy screen filter (a thin film that narrows your screen's viewing angle) costs under $30 and prevents shoulder surfing entirely.
Be aware of who is sitting near you before opening sensitive emails, documents, or financial data.
If you need to take a call involving confidential information, step outside or find a private space.

deeperLearning.title: Why physical security is often the weakest link
points: Organizations spend enormous resources on digital security, but physical exposure bypasses all of it. An unlocked screen in a shared office is a wider door than most network vulnerabilities.

Tailgating (someone following you into a secured area without badging in) and shoulder surfing (reading someone's screen nearby) are the two most common physical attack vectors in corporate environments.

The clean desk habit is also a privacy and compliance issue. Many industries — including finance, engineering, and legal — have regulatory requirements for how physical documents containing sensitive information must be handled.

checkIn.question: You're stepping away from your desk for 10 minutes. What should you do with your computer?

choices.label: Leave it open — you'll be back in a few minutes
Lock your screen before stepping away
Close the lid but don't lock it
Log out completely each time

checkIn.explanation: Always lock your screen when leaving your desk — even briefly. Windows: Win+L. Mac: Cmd+Ctrl+Q. A few seconds is all it takes for someone to access an unlocked computer.

checkIn.question: Where should you store a password you need to remember for a shared system?

choices.label: On a sticky note attached to your monitor
In a note on your phone
In an approved password manager
Written in a notebook in your desk drawer

checkIn.explanation: An approved password manager is the only secure way to store passwords. Written passwords — wherever they are — are a physical security risk.

moduleHero.title: Physical habits protect digital systems
moduleHero.description: An unlocked screen or exposed document can bypass every technical control you have in place.

redFlagSpotter.title: Spot the red flag
redFlagSpotter.prompt: You leave for a 5-minute meeting and your desk has printed client notes, an unlocked laptop, and a sticky note with a PIN. What must be fixed immediately?
redFlagSpotter.explanation: Short absences are enough for data exposure. Lock screens and secure documents every time.

password-hygiene.summary: Weak or reused passwords are involved in over 80% of confirmed data breaches. Yet most people still use the same password across multiple accounts, or choose ones that are easy to guess. Good password hygiene isn't about memorizing complex strings — it's about using the right tools and habits so you never have to trade security for convenience.

story.title: One reused password. 117 million accounts exposed.
story.meta: Credential stuffing · Password reuse · LinkedIn breach
story.text:
In 2012, LinkedIn suffered a breach that exposed 6.5 million password hashes. At the time, the company believed the damage was contained. Four years later, in 2016, the real scale emerged: 117 million credentials had actually been stolen.

What made this particularly damaging wasn't just LinkedIn. It was the fact that tens of millions of people used the same email and password combination on multiple platforms — their bank, their email, their company VPN.

Attackers used a technique called credential stuffing: taking the leaked LinkedIn username/password combinations and automatically trying them on hundreds of other websites. For every person who had reused their password, another account fell.

This is why password reuse is one of the most dangerous habits in digital security. A breach on any one platform becomes a skeleton key to everything else.

passwordStrength.title: What makes a password strong

weak.reason: Common substitutions — cracking tools test these first
Personal info — findable on social media

strong.reason: Four random words — long, memorable, takes centuries to crack
Mixed case, symbols, length — strong even without being a phrase
Generates truly random, unique passwords for every account — the best option

passwordStrength.rule: Length beats complexity. 'correct-horse-battery-staple' is stronger than 'P@$$w0rd!' — attackers know every substitution trick.

ifCompromised.title: If you think your password has been stolen
steps: Change the affected password immediately — don't wait to be sure
Change it on every other account where you used the same password
Contact IT if the compromised account is a work account — do this before changing anything so IT can investigate
Check haveibeenpwned.com to see if your email appears in known data breaches
Enable MFA on the affected account if you haven't already
Watch for unusual activity on connected accounts for the next few weeks

redFlags: Using the same password on more than one account — especially if one of them is your work email or VPN
Passwords based on personal information — birthdays, pet names, addresses — findable on social media
Passwords shorter than 12 characters
Sharing your password with a colleague to give them access to something
Not having Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) enabled on your work accounts
Storing passwords in a plain text file, a note on your phone, or a spreadsheet
responseSteps: Use an approved password manager — it creates and stores unique complex passwords for every account so you only need to remember one master password
Enable MFA on every account that supports it, starting with your Microsoft 365 work email — it's the single most effective security control available to you
Never share your password with anyone, including IT. IT staff will never ask for your password.
Use a passphrase for any account without MFA: three or four random unrelated words are more secure than any complex short password
If you suspect a work password has been compromised, contact IT immediately before changing anything — they need to investigate first

deeperLearning.title: How attackers crack passwords — and why length matters more than complexity
points: Modern password-cracking tools can test billions of combinations per second. A short complex password like 'P@ssw0rd' is cracked in under a second. A simple but long passphrase like 'correct-horse-battery-staple' takes centuries.

Credential stuffing — using leaked username/password pairs from one breach to try other sites — is fully automated and runs constantly. If you have ever reused a password, there is a meaningful chance it has already been tried somewhere.

MFA is the single most effective control against credential-based attacks. Even if an attacker has your password, they cannot access your account without the second factor you control — your phone, your authenticator app, or your hardware key.

checkIn.question: Which of the following is the strongest password?

choices.label: P@ssw0rd1!
Welcome2024
coffee-bridge-sunset-lamp
John1985!

checkIn.explanation: A long passphrase using random words is significantly stronger than a short complex password. Length matters more than symbol substitution — cracking tools test billions of combinations per second.

checkIn.question: MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication) protects your account even if your password is stolen.

choices.label: True — an attacker still needs your second factor to get in
False — a stolen password is always enough to access your account

checkIn.explanation: MFA is the single most effective control against credential-based attacks. Even with your password, an attacker cannot access your account without the second factor you control.

moduleHero.title: Reuse turns one breach into many
moduleHero.description: Unique passwords plus MFA stop credential stuffing from cascading across your accounts.

redFlagSpotter.title: Spot the red flag
redFlagSpotter.prompt: A teammate says: 'I use the same password for LinkedIn, email, and VPN because it is easier to remember.' Which risks should you flag?
redFlagSpotter.explanation: Password reuse is multiplier risk. One leaked credential pair can unlock several services.

acceptable-use.summary: PAC provides technology — computers, email, internet access, software — to help you do your job. The Acceptable Use Policy defines what these tools are for, what they are not for, and why those boundaries matter. It's not about distrust. It's about protecting you, your colleagues, and the company from risks that come from how technology gets used.

story.title: The personal device that became a company crisis
story.meta: Acceptable use · Shadow IT · Data leakage
story.text:
A project manager at a global engineering firm was frustrated that the company's approved file-sharing platform was slow. So they started using their personal Dropbox account to store and share project files — including client contracts, site drawings, and confidential cost estimates.

For months, it worked fine. Then their personal Dropbox account was compromised in a breach unrelated to work. The attacker who accessed the account found several gigabytes of the firm's confidential client data.

The company faced breach notification obligations in multiple countries. Client relationships were damaged. The project manager didn't lose their job — they were actually well-regarded — but the firm spent over $800,000 managing the fallout from a well-intentioned workaround.

This is what IT teams call shadow IT: technology used outside of approved channels that creates invisible risk. The AUP exists precisely to prevent this kind of situation.

yesNo.title: What you can and cannot do — plain answers

items.question: Can I check personal email on my work laptop?
items.detail: Generally acceptable for brief personal use, but be aware that IT can see network traffic on company devices. Don't store personal credentials in your work browser.

items.question: Can I use ChatGPT or AI tools for work tasks?
items.detail: Only if it's on the approved tools list. Never paste client data, financial information, internal project details, or confidential documents into any external AI tool. If unsure, ask IT before using it.

items.question: Can I plug a personal USB drive into my work computer?
items.detail: Personal USB drives are one of the most common ways malware enters corporate networks. Use approved file sharing platforms (SharePoint, OneDrive) instead.

items.question: Can I use my personal phone as a hotspot for work?
items.detail: Acceptable and safer than public Wi-Fi. Your phone's cellular connection is encrypted and private. Use it instead of cafe or hotel Wi-Fi.

items.question: Can I store work files on personal cloud storage (personal Dropbox, iCloud, Google Drive)?
items.detail: Personal cloud storage doesn't have PAC's security controls, encryption, or breach detection. Use only approved PAC systems (SharePoint, OneDrive for Business).

items.question: Can I install software on my work computer myself?
items.detail: All software installations must go through IT. Even trusted, free software can contain malware or create security vulnerabilities. Open an IT ticket instead.

items.question: Can I use work devices for personal side projects or freelance work?
items.detail: Work devices are for work. Personal projects create data classification issues and potential IP complications. Use a personal device for personal work.

items.question: Can I use my work email to sign up for personal accounts or newsletters?
items.detail: It's not prohibited but it's not recommended. Your work email is visible to IT, and using it for personal services creates unnecessary exposure. Use a personal email for personal services.

items.question: What is the approved platform for email, file sharing, and collaboration at PAC?
items.detail: Microsoft 365 is PAC's mandated productivity platform — Outlook, Teams, SharePoint, and OneDrive for Business. Use these for all work communication and file storage. Personal alternatives (Gmail, Dropbox, Google Drive) are not approved for work use.

items.question: Do I need to be aware of the security software on my work device?
items.detail: PAC-issued devices are protected by Acronis Cyber Protect (backup and ransomware protection) and Symantec Endpoint Protection (antivirus and threat detection). Never disable or interfere with these tools — they are mandatory. If you receive alerts from either, contact IT immediately.

consequences.title: What actually happens when AUP is violated
points: The most common consequence is not disciplinary — it's a data breach affecting you and your colleagues. The Dropbox case in this module's story resulted in client data being exposed, not just a reprimand.
In regulated industries or for roles handling personal data, individual employees can bear personal legal liability for data handling decisions — not just the company.

Intentional misuse of company systems — accessing systems you're not authorized to use, exfiltrating data, installing unauthorized software — can result in termination and in serious cases, prosecution.
The AUP exists to protect employees as much as the company. If you're using unapproved tools and something goes wrong, the organization has less ability to support you.

redFlags: Storing company data on personal cloud storage instead of approved PAC systems
Installing unapproved software on your work computer — even free, familiar tools
Using your work email to sign up for personal accounts or non-work services
Accessing company systems on personal devices without IT approval and proper security controls
Sharing confidential company or client information via personal messaging apps (WhatsApp, personal iMessage)
responseSteps: Use only PAC-approved platforms for company data — if you're unsure whether a tool is approved, ask IT before using it

Use Microsoft 365 (Outlook, Teams, SharePoint, OneDrive for Business) for all work tasks — it is PAC's mandated platform and the only productivity suite with PAC's full security controls, backup, and compliance coverage
Keep work data on work systems — SharePoint, OneDrive for Business, and approved project management tools
If an approved tool isn't meeting your needs, raise it with IT — the right answer is fixing the tool, not working around it
Never use personal accounts or devices to bypass a company security control, even temporarily
If you've already been using unapproved tools, contact IT to help you migrate — no judgment, just resolution

deeperLearning.title: Why AUP compliance protects you personally
points: When data is handled outside approved systems, the organization loses the ability to protect it. Backup, encryption, access controls, and breach detection all depend on data being where it is supposed to be.

In many jurisdictions, individual employees can bear personal legal liability for data handling decisions — not just the company. Using unapproved tools with client or employee data can have personal consequences.

The AUP is reviewed periodically. If you have a legitimate business need the current policy doesn't accommodate, the policy team wants to hear from you — it's meant to evolve with how the business actually works.

checkIn.question: The company's approved file-sharing platform is slow. What should you do?

choices.label: Use your personal Dropbox temporarily — it's faster
Email files to your personal account to work from home
Raise the issue with IT so the approved platform can be improved
Use a free transfer site just this once

checkIn.explanation: The right answer to a slow approved tool is fixing the tool — not working around it. Shadow IT creates invisible risks that bypass all organizational security controls.

checkIn.question: Using personal cloud storage for company files mainly risks:

choices.label: Slower file access speeds
Company data being exposed if your personal account is breached
Running out of storage space
Files being in the wrong format

checkIn.explanation: Personal accounts don't have the security controls, encryption, backup, and breach detection that approved PAC systems do. A personal account breach becomes a company data breach.

moduleHero.title: Approved tools are security controls
moduleHero.description: Workarounds feel efficient in the moment but create invisible data and compliance risk.

redFlagSpotter.title: Spot the red flag
redFlagSpotter.prompt: An employee moves client files to personal Dropbox because SharePoint feels slow. Which red flags apply?

flags.label: Use of unapproved storage for company data

redFlagSpotter.explanation: Intent does not remove risk. Shadow IT bypasses encryption, monitoring, and retention controls.

physical-security.summary: Physical security is the foundation that all other security controls depend on. If someone can walk into a server room, sit at an unattended computer, or access a filing cabinet — no amount of cybersecurity technology helps. Tailgating, visitor management, and USB drop attacks are among the most important and most commonly overlooked security practices in any organization.

story.title: The man who walked into 14 companies just by acting confident
story.text:
In a well-documented security audit published in 2018, a professional penetration tester was hired to test the physical security of a Fortune 500 company's offices across four cities. In one day, he walked into 14 separate buildings without a badge, an appointment, or any credentials.

His method was simple: he dressed professionally, carried a box that looked like it contained IT equipment, and waited near secure entrances for someone to badge in. Every single time, the door was held open for him. No one questioned him. In several buildings, employees even helped him carry his box to an elevator.

Once inside, he was able to access server rooms, executive offices, and workstations — in some cases leaving a physical USB device that, in a real attack, would have installed malware.

The lesson: physical security is not just IT's job. Every employee is part of the access control system.

visitorScript.title: What to say when someone doesn't have a badge
visitorScript.intro: Challenging an unfamiliar person doesn't have to be confrontational. These phrases work:

phrases.situation: Someone is following you through a secure door
phrases.say: "Sorry, our policy is that everyone needs to badge in separately — reception can help you get sorted."

phrases.situation: You see someone in a restricted area without a badge
phrases.say: "Hi there — I don't think we've met. Can I help you find who you're looking for?"

phrases.situation: A contractor or visitor is walking unescorted
phrases.say: "Hey, are you waiting for someone? I'm happy to call them for you."

phrases.situation: Someone asks to borrow your badge
phrases.say: "I can't lend my badge — it's tied to my identity in the system. Let me get someone from reception to help instead."

visitorScript.note: You are never obligated to explain PAC's security policy in detail. A friendly redirect to reception is always the right move.

usbDrop.title: USB drop attacks — don't plug in unknown devices
usbDrop.body: Attackers physically leave USB drives in car parks, reception areas, and meeting rooms with labels like 'Payroll 2024' or 'Confidential.' The curiosity is deliberate. Plugging in an unknown USB can install malware silently in seconds — you don't need to open any files. If you find an unknown USB device anywhere on PAC premises, hand it to IT without plugging it in.

redFlags: Holding a door open for someone you don't recognize — even if they look official or are carrying equipment
Allowing visitors to walk through the office unescorted
Finding a USB drive on company premises and plugging it in to see what's on it
Tailgating yourself — using someone else's badge access instead of your own
Leaving secure areas propped open for convenience
Not challenging someone who appears to be in an area they shouldn't be
responseSteps: Badge in individually every time — never hold a secure door open for someone behind you, and politely direct them to reception
All visitors must be signed in at reception and escorted at all times in secure areas — this includes contractors, maintenance workers, and delivery personnel
If you find a USB drive anywhere on PAC premises, hand it directly to IT without plugging it in — ever
If you see someone in a restricted area without a visible badge or escort, a friendly redirect to reception is appropriate and expected
Never lend your access badge to anyone, even temporarily — your badge is your identity in access logs
If your badge is lost or stolen, report it to IT and facilities immediately

deeperLearning.title: Why tailgating is so effective — and so easy to prevent
points: Tailgating works because of genuine human instinct: it feels rude not to hold a door for someone. Attackers rely on social pressure overriding security judgment.

A single uncontrolled physical access event can invalidate millions of dollars of cybersecurity investment. Once someone is physically inside a network perimeter, many digital defenses become significantly less effective.

The culture shift required is small: from 'always hold the door' to 'always badge in individually.' Most people respond well when the reason is explained — it's not about being unfriendly, it's about everyone's safety.

checkIn.question: A well-dressed person is carrying a large box and asks you to hold the door to a secure area. What do you do?

choices.label: Hold the door — it would be rude not to help
Hold the door if they look like they work there
Politely direct them to reception and badge in separately
Ask them their name before holding the door

checkIn.explanation: Every person entering a secure area must badge in individually — no exceptions. Tailgating is one of the most common physical attack methods, and it relies entirely on people being polite.

checkIn.question: You find a USB drive in the car park with 'PAC Payroll 2024' written on it. What should you do?

choices.label: Plug it in to see what's on it and return it to the right person
Hand it to IT or your security team without plugging it in
Leave it where you found it
Put it in a lost property box

checkIn.explanation: Unknown USB drives are a classic attack vector — they can install malware silently just by being plugged in. Never insert an unknown drive. Hand it directly to IT.

moduleHero.title: Doors and badges are security systems
moduleHero.description: Tailgating and unknown devices are low-tech attacks that still cause high-impact breaches.

redFlagSpotter.title: Spot the red flag
redFlagSpotter.prompt: At reception, an unfamiliar person asks you to hold a secure door while carrying equipment, and you notice no badge. What should you flag?

flags.label: No visible badge in controlled area
Request to tailgate through secure access

redFlagSpotter.explanation: Attackers often rely on politeness cues. Secure areas require individual badge authentication.

social-media.summary: Social media is one of the primary tools attackers use to research targets before a phishing or social engineering attack. Your LinkedIn profile, public posts, and online activity can reveal your role, your manager's name, current projects, travel plans, colleagues, and more — all of which can be used to craft a convincing, targeted message. This doesn't mean avoiding social media. It means being intentional about what you share.

story.title: How a LinkedIn post enabled a $2.3M fraud
story.meta: Social media · OSINT · Spear phishing · BEC
story.text:
In 2021, a finance director at a mid-sized company posted on LinkedIn celebrating the close of a major acquisition deal. They tagged their CEO and mentioned the legal firm handling the transaction.

Within days, a fraudster had used this public information to craft a highly convincing Business Email Compromise attack. They spoofed an email from the legal firm, referenced the acquisition by name, and requested an urgent wire transfer to complete a closing obligation — citing a short window before the deal terms would lapse.

The finance team wired $2.3 million before the fraud was discovered.

Every piece of information the attacker needed came from a single celebratory LinkedIn post: the company, the deal, the CEO's name, the legal firm, the deal's approximate timeline. None of it was secret. All of it was weaponized.

beforeYouPost.title: The 5-second check before you post
questions: Does this mention a client name, project name, deal value, or contract detail?
Does this reveal where I'll be, or when I won't be in the office?
Does this name a colleague, manager, or executive in a way that maps out our org structure?
Could this help someone craft a convincing impersonation of me or my company?
Has this been publicly announced, or am I the first to share it?
beforeYouPost.rule: If you answer yes to any of these — wait, or don't post. If you're not sure whether something is public yet, it isn't.

engineeringSpecific.title: What's risky for project and engineering roles specifically
points: Posting site photos, facility layouts, or construction progress images that reveal client locations or security infrastructure
Mentioning project timelines, contract values, or scope changes — even in celebration
Tagging client personnel or executives in posts about work wins
Sharing technical details about systems, equipment, or processes that competitors or attackers could exploit
Announcing travel to client sites — this signals when you'll be away and who you're meeting

redFlags: Posting about active deals, client names, project details, or financial matters on public social media
Sharing your travel schedule publicly — this signals when you won't be in the office to verify requests
Connecting with people you don't know on LinkedIn, especially those who message immediately about your work
Oversharing your org chart relationships — manager name, executive contacts, team structure
Reusing work email addresses or usernames on personal social media accounts
responseSteps: Audit your LinkedIn profile — ask whether the information you've shared could help someone impersonate a colleague or create a targeted attack
Celebrate wins internally first. Wait until information is officially public before posting externally.
Check your privacy settings on all social platforms and limit public visibility where possible
Be cautious with unsolicited LinkedIn connection requests, especially from people in vague roles with few connections
If you receive a message referencing something you shared publicly, treat it as a potential social engineering attempt and verify through a trusted channel

deeperLearning.title: OSINT — how attackers research their targets
points: OSINT (Open Source Intelligence) is the practice of gathering information from publicly available sources — social media, company websites, press releases, LinkedIn, news articles. Attackers use it systematically before launching targeted attacks.

A trained attacker can build a detailed picture of an organization's structure, current projects, key contacts, and financial activities in under an hour using only public information. The more you share publicly, the more complete that picture becomes.

This doesn't mean avoiding all social media presence — a professional online presence has real value. It means being intentional: share achievements, not operational details; connect with people you know; and think before posting about anything that could help someone impersonate a colleague.

checkIn.question: You've just closed a major deal. When is it safe to post about it on LinkedIn?

choices.label: Immediately — celebrating wins builds the company profile
Once the information is publicly announced and your manager approves
Never — all deal information must stay private permanently
After 24 hours

checkIn.explanation: Celebrate wins — but wait until the information is legitimately public and approved for sharing. Premature posts about deals, clients, or projects give attackers information they can weaponize.

checkIn.question: An attacker researching PAC employees could find which of the following on LinkedIn?

choices.label: Your system passwords
Your manager's name, role, and current projects you've mentioned
Your Microsoft 365 credentials
PAC's internal network configuration

checkIn.explanation: Attackers use publicly available information — your role, your manager, your projects, your connections — to craft convincing spear phishing attacks. Be intentional about what you share.

moduleHero.title: Public posts fuel targeted attacks
moduleHero.description: Operational details on social media help attackers craft credible spear-phishing messages.

redFlagSpotter.title: Spot the red flag
redFlagSpotter.prompt: A post says: 'Flying to client site tomorrow to finalize a confidential acquisition. Huge week for our finance team!' What is risky here?
redFlagSpotter.explanation: Attackers combine public timing, project context, and org details to build believable fraud narratives.

remote-vpn.summary: Working remotely changes your security environment significantly. Your home network, public Wi-Fi, and personal devices don't have the same protections as PAC's office infrastructure. Using the VPN, securing your home network, and being aware of your physical environment when working in public are essential habits for anyone working outside the office.

story.title: The airport lounge that became a data interception point
story.meta: Remote work · Public Wi-Fi · Man-in-the-middle attack
story.text:
A senior consultant traveling between client sites connected to an airport lounge's free Wi-Fi to catch up on emails and review a project proposal before their next meeting. The network was named something plausible — 'Lounge_WiFi_Premium' — and the connection was quick.

What they didn't know was that the network was a rogue access point set up by an attacker in the lounge. Everything they transmitted — emails, the document they was editing, their login credentials for the project management system — passed through the attacker's device before reaching the internet.

Three weeks later, the client company received a call. Someone had been accessing their project portal using the consultant's credentials. Three months of project documents — including competitive pricing strategies — had been downloaded.

All because of a free Wi-Fi connection that seemed legitimate.

vpnTroubleshoot.title: VPN won't connect — what to do
vpnTroubleshoot.intro: The most common reason employees work without the VPN is that it stopped working and they didn't know what to do next. Here's the fix:
steps: Check your internet connection first — if you can't reach any website, the issue is your connection, not the VPN
Try disconnecting and reconnecting the VPN client
Restart the VPN application completely (quit and reopen, not just minimize)
If on hotel or cafe Wi-Fi, try your phone's hotspot instead — some networks block VPN connections
Restart your computer and try again
If none of the above works, contact IT — but do not continue working on sensitive tasks without the VPN active while waiting
vpnTroubleshoot.important: If the VPN won't connect and you need to work urgently, use your phone as a personal hotspot instead of public Wi-Fi. Cellular connections are encrypted and private.

homeRouterChecklist.title: Home router security — a 10-minute fix
steps: Change the default admin password on your router (the one you use to log into its settings page at 192.168.1.1 or similar) — default passwords are widely published online
Make sure your Wi-Fi uses WPA2 or WPA3 encryption — check under your router's wireless settings. WEP is insecure and should never be used.
Change your Wi-Fi password from the default if you haven't already
Check for and apply any available firmware updates for your router
Set up a separate guest network for visitors and personal smart devices — keep work traffic on a clean network
If you're unsure how to do any of this, contact IT — they can often help remotely in 15 minutes

redFlags: Connecting to public Wi-Fi (cafes, airports, hotels) without using the PAC VPN
Working on confidential documents in public spaces where your screen can be seen
Using personal devices to access PAC systems without IT approval and proper security controls
Home router still using the default factory password
Leaving work sessions open on shared home computers used by family members
Approving VPN or MFA prompts you didn't initiate because it seemed like a glitch
responseSteps: Always connect to the PAC VPN before accessing company systems when outside the office — this encrypts your traffic and routes it securely

Disconnect from the VPN when working from the PAC office on a trusted internal network — the VPN is required for external connections, not internal ones, and staying connected on a trusted network is unnecessary
If public Wi-Fi is your only option and VPN won't connect, use your phone as a personal hotspot instead
Secure your home router: change the default admin password, use WPA2 or WPA3 encryption, and keep firmware updated
Use a screen privacy filter when working in public spaces
Lock your computer when stepping away, even at home
If the VPN won't connect and you need support, call IT — do not continue working on sensitive tasks unprotected

deeperLearning.title: How Wi-Fi attacks work — and why the VPN is your primary defence
points: A Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) attack on public Wi-Fi involves an attacker positioning themselves between your device and the internet, intercepting everything you transmit. Modern attacks can do this silently with no visible sign to the user.
Even legitimate public Wi-Fi networks in hotels and airports have minimal security. Anyone on the same network can potentially intercept unencrypted traffic.
A VPN creates an encrypted tunnel between your device and PAC's secure infrastructure. Even if someone intercepts your traffic on public Wi-Fi, they see only encrypted data they cannot read.

checkIn.question: You're at a coffee shop and need to access a confidential project document. What should you do?

choices.label: Use the café's free Wi-Fi — it's convenient and fast
Connect to the PAC VPN first, then access the document
Use the café Wi-Fi but only look at non-sensitive files
Wait until you're home to access any work files

checkIn.explanation: Always connect to the PAC VPN before accessing company systems outside the office. The VPN encrypts your traffic so that even if someone intercepts it on public Wi-Fi, they see only unreadable data.

checkIn.question: Why is your home Wi-Fi network potentially risky for work without a VPN?

choices.label: Home networks are always slower than office networks
Home routers often have weaker security settings and default passwords
Working from home is against company policy
Home networks can't support encrypted connections

checkIn.explanation: Many home routers still use default passwords and older encryption standards. Without a VPN, traffic on your home network can potentially be intercepted if your router is compromised.

moduleHero.title: Remote convenience needs stronger controls

ai-acceptable-use.summary: PAC has approved specific AI tools for specific uses. AI tools that process your input may store that data on external servers, use it to train models, or expose it to third parties — often permanently. One employee pasting the wrong document into a public AI tool can expose confidential client data, proprietary project details, or personal information in seconds with no way to retrieve it. This module explains what you can use, what you cannot, and why data classification is the most important concept to understand before using any AI tool.

story.title: The engineers who leaked source code to an AI — and sparked a global policy change
story.meta: AI security · Data leakage · Samsung breach 2023
story.text:
In March 2023, engineers at Samsung's semiconductor division began using ChatGPT to help with their work. Within weeks, three separate incidents occurred: one engineer pasted proprietary source code into ChatGPT to ask it to fix bugs. Another uploaded internal meeting notes. A third used it to convert confidential test data into a presentation format.

In each case, the data left Samsung's systems and was transmitted to OpenAI's servers — where, under the terms of service at the time, it could be used to train future models and potentially seen by OpenAI staff reviewing outputs.

Samsung banned all external AI tools within days. But by then, the proprietary code, internal meeting content, and confidential test data were already on external servers beyond Samsung's control.

This is the fundamental risk of AI tools: they are helpful, they are fast, and they are invisible data pipelines to the outside world.

dataClassification.title: PAC's Data Classification Framework — know before you share
dataClassification.intro: Before using any AI tool, classify what you're working with. The classification determines whether you can use AI at all — and which tool is appropriate.

tiers.label: PUBLIC
tiers.name: Public information
tiers.description: Information approved for public release: published press releases, publicly announced project completions, general marketing materials.
tiers.aiRule: AI tools may be used with Public data — no restrictions apply.

tiers.label: PRIVATE
tiers.name: Private / Internal information
tiers.description: Internal information not intended for public disclosure: employee information, internal processes, operational data, budget summaries, internal project status.
tiers.aiRule: Only approved AI tools (Microsoft Copilot within M365) may be used with Private data. External AI tools are not approved.

tiers.label: RESTRICTED
tiers.name: Restricted / Confidential information
tiers.description: Highly sensitive information: client data, contracts, financial records, legal documents, personal information, security credentials, proprietary designs.
tiers.aiRule: No AI tools — internal or external — may receive Restricted data without explicit IT approval.

yesNo.title: What you can and cannot do — plain answers

items.question: Can I use Microsoft Copilot in M365 (Outlook, Teams, Word) for work tasks?
items.detail: Microsoft Copilot within PAC's M365 environment is the approved AI tool for work. It operates within PAC's existing security boundary and is subject to PAC's data controls and compliance framework.

items.question: Can I use ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, or other public AI tools for work tasks?
items.detail: Only for Public data or generic non-confidential tasks (drafting general templates, explaining general concepts). Never input client data, financial information, project details, contracts, or any Private or Restricted information. If in doubt, use Copilot instead.

items.question: Can I paste a client document into an AI tool to summarize it?
items.detail: Client documents are Restricted data. Pasting them into any external AI tool transmits that data to third-party servers outside PAC's control, permanently. Use Microsoft Copilot within M365 only — and even then, confirm the document's classification first.

items.question: Can I use AI to help write code for work projects?
items.detail: Acceptable if the code does not contain PAC-specific credentials, API keys, proprietary algorithms, client system details, or confidential architecture. Strip out anything sensitive before using an external AI tool. Copilot in M365 is preferred.

items.question: Can I share PAC financial data or HR information with an AI tool?
items.detail: Financial records and HR data are Restricted. They must never be entered into any AI tool — including Microsoft Copilot — without explicit IT and management authorization.

items.question: Can I use AI-generated content in client deliverables?
items.detail: Only after thorough review. AI tools can produce plausible but factually incorrect output. Any AI-assisted content used in client work must be reviewed and verified by a qualified person before delivery. Ensure no confidential data was used to generate it.

consequences.title: What happens when AI policy is violated
points: Data transmitted to an external AI tool cannot be retrieved. Once client data, financial records, or proprietary information leaves PAC's systems, it is permanently outside your control — regardless of the AI tool's privacy policy.

PAC may have legal obligations to notify clients and regulators if their confidential information is disclosed to a third party — even inadvertently. This can result in contract termination and significant legal liability.

Individual employees can bear personal liability for data handling decisions. Sharing client data with unauthorised third-party tools can constitute a breach of data protection law or contractual confidentiality obligations.
Intentional violation of the AI Acceptable Use Policy — particularly sharing Restricted data — may result in disciplinary action up to and including termination.

redFlags: Pasting client names, project details, contract terms, or financial data into any external AI tool
Using ChatGPT, Gemini, or similar tools to summarise, translate, or reformat confidential documents
Sharing PAC credentials, API keys, or system architecture details with any AI tool
Using a personal AI subscription for work tasks that involve any Private or Restricted data
Using AI-generated content in client deliverables without reviewing it for accuracy
Connecting third-party AI plugins or browser extensions to PAC systems without IT approval
responseSteps: Before using any AI tool, classify your data: Public (external AI tools allowed), Private (Copilot in M365 only), or Restricted (no AI without IT approval)
Use Microsoft Copilot within PAC's M365 environment as your primary AI tool — it is approved, supported, and operates within PAC's security boundary
For external AI tools (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini), use only for generic or Public tasks — never input anything client-related, financial, or project-specific
Review all AI-generated content before using it in any work product — AI tools can produce plausible but factually incorrect output
If you're unsure whether a task or data type is AI-appropriate, ask IT before proceeding — not after
If you believe you've shared Restricted or Private data with an unauthorised AI tool, report it to IT immediately — early disclosure limits damage

deeperLearning.title: How AI tools handle your data — and why the boundary matters
points: Most public AI tools (free ChatGPT, Gemini, etc.) may use inputs to improve their models unless you explicitly opt out — and even paid tiers may retain inputs for safety review. When you paste a confidential document, you are not just asking a question. You are uploading data to a third-party server with its own terms of service, retention policies, and potential future disclosures.

Microsoft Copilot within PAC's M365 environment is different: it is bound by PAC's Microsoft data processing agreement, subject to the same retention and deletion policies as your work email, and does not use PAC's data to train public models. This is why it is the approved tool — the data boundary is controlled.

The PAC Data Classification Framework (Public, Private, Restricted) applies to every decision about where data goes — cloud storage, email, USB drives, printed documents, and AI tools. AI tools create a fast-moving new channel through which data can leave the organisation. The classification gives you a consistent rule regardless of the technology.

checkIn.question: You need to summarise a client contract to prepare for a meeting. Which approach is correct?

choices.label: Paste the contract into ChatGPT — it's faster and the summary is just for you
Use Microsoft Copilot within M365 — client contracts are Restricted data
Use any AI tool as long as you don't share the summary externally
Email the contract to a colleague to summarise it instead

checkIn.explanation: Client contracts are Restricted data. Only Microsoft Copilot within PAC's M365 environment is approved for this use. External AI tools like ChatGPT transmit data to third-party servers permanently — there is no way to retrieve it.

checkIn.question: Under PAC's Data Classification Framework, which type of data may be used with external AI tools (ChatGPT, Gemini, etc.)?

choices.label: Private — internal processes and employee information
Restricted — client data and financial records
Public — information already approved for public release
All data, as long as you use a paid AI subscription

checkIn.explanation: Only Public data may be used with external AI tools. Private data requires Microsoft Copilot in M365. Restricted data requires explicit IT approval — and even then, no external AI tools.

moduleHero.title: Data classification comes before AI prompts
moduleHero.description: If you cannot classify data confidently, do not paste it into any AI system.

redFlagSpotter.title: Spot the red flag
redFlagSpotter.prompt: A user pastes client contract clauses and financial terms into a public AI tool to get a summary. Which problems are present?
redFlagSpotter.explanation: Restricted data must stay within approved boundaries. External AI use can create irreversible disclosure risk.

quickTakeaway.title: 1-minute takeaway
points: If something feels off, report now — don't wait for proof.
If you clicked or entered credentials, contact IT immediately.
Fast reporting limits damage; silence expands it.

microScenario.title: Quick decision check
microScenario.question: You clicked a suspicious link, entered your credentials, and then the page looked broken. What should you do in the next 5 minutes?

choices.label: Delete the email and monitor quietly
Change password alone and tell no one
Report via Barracuda and call/message IT immediately

microScenario.bestAction: Correct move: report immediately and contact IT directly so containment starts while the incident is still small.

incident-reporting.summary: Incident reporting is your fastest security control. A click, a suspicious login, or a lost device is recoverable when reported early. The real risk is delay. At PAC, reporting is no-blame: we care about fast response, not perfect decisions.

story.title: The breach that took 206 days to discover — because no one reported it
story.meta: Incident reporting · Dwell time · Delayed response
story.text:
In a widely studied cybersecurity case, a retail company was compromised when an employee clicked a phishing link. The employee realized almost immediately that something had felt wrong about the email — the site had asked for their credentials and then seemed to error out.

They were embarrassed. They thought they'd probably imagined it, or that it wasn't a big deal. They didn't report it.

The attacker spent 206 days inside the network before being detected by an external security researcher. By that point, 56 million customer payment card records had been exfiltrated. The total cost of the breach exceeded $250 million.

The employee who clicked the link was never blamed. The investigation concluded that if they had reported the incident on day one, the attacker could have been evicted before any customer data was compromised.

Reporting is not the last line of defense. It is often the only line of defense that still works after an attack has started.

barracuda.title: How to report using Barracuda — step by step
steps: Open the suspicious email in Microsoft Outlook — do not click any links or open any attachments first
Look for the Barracuda button in your Outlook ribbon at the top of the screen — it appears as a Barracuda icon in the Home tab
Click the Barracuda button — a dialog will appear asking you to confirm the report
Select the reason that best fits (Phishing, Spam, or Suspicious) and click Submit
The email will be automatically forwarded to PAC's IT Security team and to Barracuda's threat intelligence network
You can safely delete the email after reporting — Barracuda has already captured it
barracuda.cantFindIt: If you cannot find the Barracuda button in your ribbon, contact IT to have it installed. In the meantime, forward the suspicious email to phishing@pacgroup.com as an attachment.
barracuda.afterYouReport: After you click report, here is what happens: IT receives an automatic notification within minutes. If the email is confirmed as a phishing campaign, IT will alert the wider organization. If your credentials may have been compromised, IT will contact you directly to guide you through securing your account. You will not be in trouble for reporting — even if it turns out to be a false alarm.

whatHappensNext.title: What happens after you report — the full process
steps: IT receives your report automatically via Barracuda within minutes
The email is analysed — IT determines whether it is phishing, spam, or legitimate
If it is a confirmed phishing attempt, IT checks whether anyone else in the organization received the same email
If a wider campaign is detected, IT sends a warning to affected employees
If you clicked a link or entered credentials, IT will contact you directly to help secure your account — this is supportive, not disciplinary
The threat intelligence is shared with Barracuda to protect other organizations too

whenInDoubt.title: When in doubt — report it anyway
whenInDoubt.body: The threshold for reporting should be zero. If something feels even slightly off — the sender seems unusual, the request is unexpected, the link destination looks strange, the tone is different from normal — report it. IT would rather receive 100 false alarms than miss one real attack. There is no such thing as over-reporting a security concern at PAC.

redFlags: You clicked a link and the page looked wrong, failed oddly, or asked for unexpected credentials
You opened an attachment and your device started acting unusually
You replied to or acted on a suspicious request before realizing it
A work device or storage media is lost, stolen, or unaccounted for
You notice account activity you did not initiate
responseSteps: Report immediately using Barracuda in Outlook (or your approved reporting route).
If credentials may be exposed, contact IT directly right away — don't rely on reporting alone.
Do not self-remediate first (no deleting, wiping, or ad-hoc fixes) until IT advises.
Capture quick facts while fresh: what happened, when, and what you clicked/opened.
For lost/stolen devices, notify IT and your manager immediately so containment starts fast.
Assume no blame for honest mistakes; fast reporting is the expected behavior.

deeperLearning.title: Why speed beats certainty
points: Attackers cause most damage after initial access, not at first contact. Early reporting cuts that window down.
IT can isolate accounts, devices, and campaigns quickly only if they know early.
No-blame reporting isn't just culture — it's a practical defense mechanism.

checkIn.question: You clicked a link in an email and the page asked for your credentials. You entered them before realizing it looked suspicious. What do you do?

choices.label: Change your password quietly and hope nothing happens
Wait to see if anything unusual happens before reporting
Contact IT immediately and report what happened
Delete the email and the browser history

checkIn.explanation: Report immediately. The goal is fast containment, not silent cleanup.

checkIn.question: PAC operates a no-blame incident reporting culture. What does this mean in practice?

choices.label: Mistakes are ignored and never investigated
If you report an incident honestly, you will be supported — not punished
Only IT staff are required to report security incidents
Reports are only needed for serious breaches, not minor incidents

checkIn.explanation: No-blame means early reporting is encouraged and supported — especially when you're unsure.

moduleHero.title: Speed is the control
moduleHero.description: Early reporting contains incidents; silence gives attackers time to expand impact.

redFlagSpotter.title: Spot the red flag
redFlagSpotter.prompt: You clicked a suspicious link and entered credentials, then decide to delete the email and wait. What should be flagged?
redFlagSpotter.explanation: Containment depends on immediate reporting. Quiet self-remediation delays response and increases blast radius.
